title: Roman argument: Christ would have expressly commanded writing
source_text: X. Praeterea Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, ut probent verbum Dei Ecclesiae necessarium latius patere quam Scripturam sacram, sic ratiocinantur. Si Christo & Apostolis fuisset propositum verbum Dei coarctare & restringere ad Scripturam sacram, rem tanti momenti Christus aperte praecepisset. Et Apostoli testarentur se ex Domini mandato scribere, quemadmodum ex Domini mandato toto orbe docuerunt: Sed id nusquam legimus.
pass_a_gloss: Moreover the Doctors of the Roman Church, to prove that the Word of God necessary to the Church extends more widely than sacred Scripture, reason thus. If it had been Christ's and the Apostles' purpose to confine and restrict the Word of God to sacred Scripture, Christ would have openly commanded a matter of such moment. And the Apostles would testify that they write by the Lord's command, just as they taught throughout the whole world by the Lord's command: But we nowhere read that.
pass_b_english: Rome's next move: if Scripture alone were the Word, Christ would have plainly ordered writing.
They want an explicit 'write this' parallel to the explicit 'teach the nations' mandate.
Because they find no such vocal command on the page, they say the Word outruns the book.
The claim sets up the reply: inspiration itself is the stronger mandate.

lemmas.gloss: narrow the Word to Scripture alone
we nowhere read such a command
